q: In which order does Kruskal's algorithm consider the edges?
options: In BFS order from a start vertex
In the order they are given
explain: Sorting is the first step. Cheap edges are tried first, and each is kept unless it would close a cycle.

q: When does Kruskal reject an edge (u, v)?
options: When u and v are already in the same component (the edge would form a cycle)
When u has already been used by another edge
When the edge is heavier than the previous one
explain: Only same-component edges close a cycle. One endpoint having other edges does not matter.

q: Which data structure makes Kruskal's cycle test fast?
explain: find tells you which component a vertex is in, and union merges two components after an edge is accepted.

q: What is the running time of Kruskal's algorithm?
options: O(E log E), dominated by sorting
explain: Sorting costs O(E log E). With union by rank and path compression, the union–find work is almost linear, O(E α(V)).

q: What does path compression do in find(x)?
options: Makes every node on the path from x point directly to the root
Moves x to the root position
explain: Later finds on those nodes become one step. Combined with union by rank, the amortised cost per operation is α(n), which is effectively constant.

q: In the page example, which edges does Kruskal reject?
explain: When the weight-4 edges are reached, A, B, C and D are already connected, and so are E, F and G. All three of those edges would close cycles. C–E 5 is then accepted, and the algorithm stops with 6 edges.

q: Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms always give MSTs of the same total weight on the same connected graph.
explain: True. Both find a minimum spanning tree, and all MSTs share the same minimum weight. They may pick different edges when weights tie.

q: During Kruskal, before it finishes, what does the set of accepted edges form?
explain: Accepted edges can be far apart in the graph, so the partial result is a forest that merges into one tree at the end. Prim, by contrast, always has one tree.

q: How can Kruskal's algorithm be stopped early to split points into k clusters?
options: Stop when exactly k components remain
Stop at the k-th heaviest edge
Sort in decreasing order and take k edges
explain: Each accepted edge merges two clusters. Stopping at k components leaves the k clusters as far apart as possible: this is single-linkage clustering.

q: A graph has V vertices. When can Kruskal stop scanning edges?
options: As soon as V − 1 edges have been accepted
Only after every edge has been examined
explain: A spanning tree has exactly V − 1 edges. Once that many have been accepted, every remaining edge would close a cycle.
